title: Waldo Canyon Wildfire Containment Efforts
description: Fort Carson personnel help battle the wildfires that threaten the US Air Force academy.  Soundbites include Lt. Col. Danielle Ngo - Commander, 52nd Engineer Battalion; Ken Helgerson - Deputy Fire Chief, Air Force Academy; JT Mcleod - Fort Carson Fire Emergency Services, Task Force leader; SFC. Justin Payne - 4th Engineer Battalion, Horizontal Construction Engineer and SFC. Brian Rethage - 52nd Engineer Battalion, Construction Equipment Supervisor.  Produced by CPL. Anthony Kozleuchar.  Also available in High Definition.
keywords: Fort Carson, Wildfire, Anthony Kozleuchar, Coloradofire, Waldo Canyon, Danielle Ngo, Ken Helgerson, JT Mcleod, Justin Payne, Brian Rethage, AIr Force, Fire, High Definition, troops, civilians, Air Force Academy

transcript.text: We had already prepared all of our equipment, our personnel were prepared, and as soon as we were called,
and given the go-ahead, we left. And we know the sense of urgency. We have our soldiers and our
equipment still prepared to provide additional assistance whenever it's needed. The response here
from the Air Force Academy to receive us has been wonderful. It's a team, the Air Force Academy,
and us. We work well together on a normal basis. They're our sister service. We're going to support
them, and they support us. So when we got called out here to help all our soldiers were so enthusiastic
that they could help, a real-world mission, help the Air Force Academy, our sister service, and
be a part of this team that hopefully will spare lives and spare people's homes.
Right. We actually asked our EOC for some additional support for dozers, and we got a huge footprint
of Army resources in here, and probably three times the amount of dozers that I thought were
available. And they came in here and basically we asked for them at, I think, nine o'clock in the
morning, and they were here by the time the sun went down, fully mobilized, and they started working
last night before the sun even went down. And they started at first light this morning, and we're
able to get a lot of work in just a short amount of time. We have the folks in the front line attacking
the fire. There's a lot of folks in Fort Carson here. They've supported us with quite a few fire
engines designed for this kind of purpose, quite a few people who are especially trained in
while in firefighting. And they've actually have a whole division of our footprint here in attacking
the fire and making sure it doesn't continue across the academy. So basically those were the
two main constructs of the support we got from the Fort Carson folks. And on both ends, it's been a huge
value to us to have those resources available. Our appreciation for our neighboring agencies,
specifically Fort Carson, have been priceless in terms of defending the Air Force Academy property
from this wildfire. As of Tuesday evening when we had the big blow up here on the west side of
Colorado Springs, this task force has been going almost day and night. The first night, as I said,
before they were in this division here, right to the south of us, we did structure protection,
burned out around structures, put out backing fires that were right alongside the road, pretty much
right in the thick of things. The Air Force Academy has been on Fort Carson many, many times
helping us. So his Colorado Springs Fire Department, so is El Paso County. So has Shine Mountain. We
have an excellent, excellent rapport with the county and city departments around us
because of that reason, because all of us need help at certain times. My soldiers are doing
excellent, really proud of them. And it's really wonderful working with the joint task force of
the Air Force Academy and the local fire departments and all the different law enforcement agencies
that help us get up here through the roads, you know, negotiate all the traffic and all that kind of
stuff. It just shows what we can do as a cohesive team. It shows that when we come together and we
got our mind on something, you know, we can handle business. We take care of it, we execute,
or professional, we do it together. And then we go ahead and go back to our normal daily lives.
It's all one team, one fight when it comes down to it. So it doesn't matter what branch of service
you're in, we all have the same end state and then we're all here to get each other's back.
